01.r: Menahem made the silver come out of his people's hands.
01.n: The form is causative: literally 'he made (it) go out', 'he brought out'; YLT keeps 'bringeth out'. The 'And' at the head of our sentence belongs to this verb. The KJV's 'exacted' is not used here, because our register keeps 'exact' for the creditor's verb.

02.r: The king of Israel who paid off Assyria.
02.n: Gesenius: the name means 'comforter', and he was a king of Israel, citing 2 Ki. 15:17 to 22.

03.r: Marks 'the silver' as the object of the verb.
03.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'the silver'.

04.r: The silver needed to pay the Assyrian king.
04.n: The word is the metal, and so money; our register renders it 'silver' throughout. The article makes it a particular sum: the silver this payment required.

05.r: The levy is laid on Israel as a burden.
05.n: The preposition means 'upon': the charge rests on the people. YLT and the BSB say 'from', which gives where the silver came from rather than on whom it fell.

06.r: The northern kingdom that Menahem ruled.

07.r: Narrows the levy: it fell on the wealthy.
07.n: The same preposition is repeated to say who in Israel bore the charge.

08.r: No wealthy man was left out.

09.r: Men of standing in the land.
09.n: Gesenius gives first 'strong, mighty', commonly of a soldier, a hero. Joined to the next word it names men strong in wealth rather than in battle.

10.r: Their riches, which made them liable to the levy.
10.n: Gesenius gives first 'strength, power, might', and then forces, a host; the brief's lexicon lists wealth among its senses. Here 'mighty men of wealth' are men strong in means, and the Greek translators took the word as 'strength'.

11.r: The purpose of the levy: payment to Assyria.

12.r: The silver is for a foreign king.

13.r: The empire pressing on Israel from the north east.

14.r: The amount laid on each wealthy man.

15.r: A weight of silver used as money.
15.n: Gesenius: a certain weight of gold and silver, which the Hebrews used, when weighed, for money. There was no coin; the silver was weighed out.

17.r: Every wealthy man paid the same amount.
17.n: Literally 'to one man': the Hebrew says 'man' and 'one', which together mean 'each'. This phrase covers both words.

18.r: One at a time, every man alike.
18.n: The number 'one', used here to mean 'each'; counted with 'for each man'.

19.r: Paid off, the Assyrian king left.
19.n: Gesenius: to turn about, to return. The 'And' before 'the king' belongs to this verb.

21.r: The empire bought off by the levy.

23.r: He did not hold his ground in Israel.
23.n: The verb's first sense is 'to stand'; here, to stay put.

01.n: Swete's ἐξήνεγκεν is the aorist of ἐκφέρω, to carry out, bring out, which the brief leaves without a dictionary form. It keeps the Hebrew picture: he brought the silver out.

04.n: ἀργύριον, silver (money), the word our register renders 'silver'.

10.n: ἰσχύς, strength: the Greek reads 'every man mighty in strength', taking the Hebrew word in its first sense rather than as wealth.

15.n: σίκλος, the Greek form of 'shekel'. The Greek has no word for 'silver' after it.
